---
title: "Discrete and Continuous: Two Choices"
---

A sound wave varies through time. A recorder takes a reading every fraction of a second and stores one of a finite collection of numerical codes.

Two choices have occurred: where to observe, and which values to distinguish.

Both can be discrete or continuous.

## 🔰 Ask about the domain and the values separately {#sec-sample-discrete-and-continuous-ask-about-the-domain-and-the-values-separately}

A discrete observation domain has individually indexed addresses. A continuous-time model allows a value to be specified at every time in an interval.

The value alphabet is a different question:

- A die observed at numbered trials has a discrete domain and discrete values.
- An ideal real-valued sensor sampled once per second has a discrete domain and a continuous value model.
- An ideal switch monitored at every time has a continuous domain and values in $\{0,1\}$.
- An ideal voltage waveform has a continuous domain and a continuous value model.

A continuous domain does not require a continuous function. The switch can jump.

Likewise, a continuous value model does not imply that a stored computer number has infinitely many bits. The mathematical model and its numerical representation have different resolutions.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sample-domain-values
#| fig-cap: "Sampling changes the available addresses; quantization changes the available values. Either can be applied independently."
#| fig-alt: "Four plots show a smooth signal, samples of that signal, the signal rounded to integer levels, and samples rounded to integer levels."
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

dense_times = np.linspace(0, 4, 801)
sample_times = np.arange(0, 4.01, 0.5)
dense_values = 1.2 + 0.8 * np.sin(np.pi * dense_times / 2)
sample_values = 1.2 + 0.8 * np.sin(np.pi * sample_times / 2)
figure, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 6), layout="constrained")
axes[0, 0].plot(dense_times, dense_values, color="#236B8E")
axes[0, 1].stem(sample_times, sample_values, basefmt=" ")
axes[1, 0].step(
    dense_times, np.rint(dense_values), where="mid", color="#A54B30"
)
axes[1, 1].stem(sample_times, np.rint(sample_values), basefmt=" ")
titles = [
    "Continuous time, real-valued model",
    "Sampled time, real-valued model",
    "Continuous time, quantized values",
    "Sampled time, quantized values"
]
for axis, title in zip(axes.flat, titles):
    axis.set(title=title, xlabel="Time", ylabel="Value", ylim=(-0.2, 2.4))
    axis.grid(alpha=0.15)
plt.show()
```

## 🏵 Sampling and quantization have different jobs {#sec-sample-discrete-and-continuous-sampling-and-quantization-have-different-jobs}

For a continuous-time signal $x(t)$, sampling at an interval $\Delta t>0$ produces

$$
S[k]=x(k\Delta t).
$$

Quantization applies a rule $Q$ to the values:

$$
D[k]=Q(S[k]).
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer is one quantizer. Thresholding into “low” and “high” is another. Both merge values that the previous representation could distinguish.

Sampling can miss changes between addresses. Quantization can hide changes within a value bin. Improving one resolution does not automatically improve the other.

## ⚙️ Counting addresses and measuring duration {#sec-sample-discrete-and-continuous-counting-addresses-and-measuring-duration}

Four observations at times $0,1,2,3$ seconds give

$$
n=4,\qquad
\text{elapsed span}=3\text{ seconds}.
$$

The count and the elapsed span answer different questions.

Similarly, summing four temperatures does not produce a time integral. An approximation to an integral needs interval widths and an agreed rule for which reading represents each interval:

$$
\int_a^b x(t)\,dt
\ \approx\
\sum_k x(t_k)\,\Delta t_k.
$$

Those interval weights carry units of time. They explain why adding more sample points should not, by itself, double the physical area under a fixed waveform.

## 💡 Discrete does not mean finite {#sec-sample-discrete-and-continuous-discrete-does-not-mean-finite}

The whole numbers form a discrete, countably infinite collection. A continuous interval can have finite length. “How many?” and “how much length?” use different measures.

We will use this distinction again in [Probability](probability.qmd): point masses are accumulated by sums, while densities are accumulated against a measure such as interval length.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-discrete-and-continuous-try-the-idea}

A thermostat reads every second and reports either “cold” or “warm.” Which part is sampling, which is quantization, and what improvement would preserve small temperature changes?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-discrete-and-continuous-work-it-through}

Reading every second samples the time domain. Reporting two labels quantizes the values. Retaining more temperature levels can preserve smaller changes in value; recording more often addresses changes between readings.
:::
